en: Oṃ. Salutation to the Brahman that is *tat-sat*. Oṃ! May my limbs, speech, breath, eye, ear, and also my strength and all my senses be nourished. May I not abandon the Veda; may the Veda not abandon me. May there be no abandonment, may there be no abandonment for me. May those qualities which reside in the self and are found in the Upaniṣads be in me; may they be in me.

Oṃ. Peace! Peace! Peace! The commencement of the ninth chapter is as follows: it must be stated that the Upaniṣad beginning with "By whom impelled" (*keneṣita*) has the Supreme Brahman as its subject matter. Prior to this, ritual actions (*karmāṇi*) have been completed in their entirety, and the meditations (*upāsanāni*) upon Prāṇa—the substratum of all rituals—have been taught, as well as those concerning the Sāmans that are auxiliary parts of the rituals. Subsequently, the vision (*darśana*) concerning the Gāyatra Sāman, ending with the lineage (*vaṃśa*), has been declared as that which is to be performed.

All this aforementioned action and knowledge, when properly performed by one who is free from desire and seeks liberation, serve for the purpose of purifying the *sattva*. However, for one who possesses desire and is devoid of knowledge, mere ritual acts prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* lead to the path of the right-hand way and to rebirth. But through natural activity that is not in accordance with the scriptures, there would be a downward course ending in the state of animals and stationary beings.

For it is stated in the Śruti: "Now, those who do not travel by either of these two paths become these small, repeatedly returning beings; 'be born and die'—this is the third station"; and also from the mantra-text: "Three classes of creatures have passed beyond this limit."

However, for one whose being is purified and who is indeed free from desire—having become dispassionate toward the impermanent relationship between means and ends, whether performed here in this life or previously—and having arisen from a particular refinement (*saṃskāra*), the desire to know the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) proceeds. This very matter is demonstrated by the Śruti through the form of questions and answers, beginning with "By whom impelled? (Kena Upaniṣad 1.1). And it is said in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "The Self-existent pierced the openings outward; therefore, one looks outward, not at the inner Self."

"A certain wise man, desiring immortality, beheld the inner Self with his eyes turned away [from the external]," and so forth; and in the Atharva Veda: "Having examined the worlds acquired through action, a Brahmin should attain detachment, realizing that 'there is nothing uncreated [eternal] to be gained by what is created. For the sake of knowing That, he should approach a Guru alone, carrying fuel in his hand—a learned Śrotriya established in Brahman. And so on.

For it is only for one who is thus dispassionate that the capacity to hear, reflect upon, and realize the knowledge concerning the inner Self (pratyagātman) becomes possible, and not otherwise. And from this realization of the Brahman as the inner Self, ignorance—the seed of saṃsāra and the cause of the engagement in desire and action—is entirely removed, according to the Vedic mantra: "What delusion, what sorrow can there be for him who perceives oneness? and the scriptural statement: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and "The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are rent asunder."
And from such scriptural passages as, "His actions perish when He, who is both high and low, has been seen.

If it is argued that this [liberation] is established even by knowledge conjoined with action, we say no; because in the Vājasaneyaka, it is stated that those are causes for something else. Having introduced the topic with, "May I have a wife," it is said in the Vājasaneyaka: "This world is to be won by a son, not by any other action; the world of the fathers by action; the world of the gods by knowledge. Thus, in the Vājasaneyaka, the causality of three worlds distinct from the Self is declared.

And in that very injunction for wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), the reason is stated: "What shall we do with offspring, for us this Self is this world? Therein, the meaning of this reason is as follows: what shall we accomplish with offspring, ritual action, and the knowledge associated with them—which are the means for attaining the three worlds of humans, ancestors, and gods, and which serve as causes for failing to attain the world of the Self?

Furthermore, we do not maintain that the three worlds—which are impermanent—are to be accomplished by means of spiritual practices. For us, the world is held to be innate, unborn, undecaying, immortal, fearless, neither increased by action nor diminished; it is eternal. And because it is eternal, it cannot be produced by any other means apart from the cessation of ignorance. Therefore, preceded by the realization of Brahman as the inner Self, one must perform the renunciation of all desires.

Furthermore, due to the contradiction with the coexistence of action, it is not possible for the knowledge of the inner self as Brahman—which has as its object the inner self as Brahman, in which all perceptions of difference have subsided—to coexist with ritual action that involves the cognition of a distinction between agents and results. This is because, when the reality of the thing itself is primary, the knowledge of Brahman is independent of the person (the agent).

Therefore, for one who is dispassionate toward the seen and the unseen—that which is accomplished by means of the body and its organs—this inquiry into Brahman concerning the inner Self (*pratyagātman*) is presented by the scripture beginning with "By whom impelled? The presentation in the form of questions and answers between a disciple and a teacher serves as a cause for easy comprehension, because the subject matter is subtle; furthermore, it demonstrates that [Brahman] is not accessible through mere logic alone.

And because of the Vedic text, "This wisdom is not to be attained through reasoning," and because of the restrictive injunctions of Śruti and Smṛti such as, "The man who has a teacher knows," "From the teacher alone one obtains knowledge, which, when known, leads most effectively to the goal," and "Learn that by prostration," it is inferred that someone, having approached a Guru established in Brahman according to the rules and seeing no refuge other than the subject of the inner Self, asked [this question] while desiring the fearless, eternal, auspicious, and immovable state.
Oṃ! By whom impelled does the mind fly forth when sent? By whom joined does the first breath proceed? By whom impelled do they speak this speech? And which god joins the eye and the ear? 1.

"By whom impelled, by which agent impelled, does the mind fly—that is, go—toward its own object? This is the connection. Since the sense of repetition (*ābhīkṣṇya*) or motion for the root *iṣ* is impossible here, it is understood that this form belongs solely to the sense of "desiring. The use of the form *iṣitam* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). Of that same root, when preceded by *pra*, in the sense of "commanding," we have the form *preṣitam*.

In that context, if only "impelled" (*praṣita*) were said, there would arise an expectation for the specific details of the impeller and the impulse—namely, by what kind of impeller, or of what nature is the impulse? However, when the qualification "willed" (*iṣita*) is present, both of those [expectations] are removed, because the specific meaning is determined as "impelled by whose mere will.

If this were the intended meaning, it would have been established by the word "by whom willed" (*keneṣita*) alone; thus, it would be appropriate to understand the specific meaning as "by whom was it impelled," whether by will, by action, or by speech.

No, because of the force of the question itself. It is logical [to conclude] from the force of the context that one who is detached from the transitory body-complex—which is the effect of karma—and who desires to know another reality that is immutable and eternal, asks this question. Otherwise, since it is well known that the body-complex is impelled by will, speech, and action, the question would be entirely purposeless. Even so, the meaning of the word "impelled" (*preṣita*) has not yet been demonstrated.

No; since this question arises from one who has a doubt, the specific meaning of the word "impelled" (*preṣita*) is appropriate. Is the state of being an impeller (*preṣayitṛtva*) of the aggregate of body and organs as it is commonly understood, or rather, does it belong to one distinct from that aggregate—a self-sufficient entity who impels the mind and so forth by mere will? It is for the purpose of demonstrating this point that the two qualifications, "that by which the mind is impelled when it is sent forth" and "that by which it falls when it is impelled," are appropriate.

Now, it is well known that the mind is independent and falls of its own accord upon its own objects; how, then, is a question regarding this appropriate? It is said in reply: if the mind were independent with respect to its engagement and withdrawal, then no one would ever think of what is undesirable. Furthermore, it would not form intentions while knowing them to be harmful. Moreover, even when restrained, the mind would still engage in actions that result in immediate suffering. Therefore, the question beginning with "By whom impelled... and so forth is indeed appropriate.

By whom is the primary breath—being joined, directed, and impelled—set forth toward its own function? "The first" is an epithet of the breath, because all activities of the senses are preceded by it. By whom impelled do people utter this speech characterized by sound? Likewise, which radiant deity joins, directs, and impels the eye and the ear toward their respective objects? || 1 ||

To the qualified one who has thus questioned him, the Guru says: "Listen to that which you ask: who is the deity that impels the collection of instruments beginning with the mind toward their respective objects, and how does he impel them? He is the hearer of the ear, the thinker of the mind, the speaker of speech, and the breath of the breath; he is the seer of the eye. Having transcended these, the wise, departing from this world, become immortal. (2)

"The ear of the ear"—it is called the "ear" because one hears by means of it; it is the organ of hearing, the instrument for the perception of sound, that which manifests sound. Its "ear" is that which you asked about when you asked, "Which god joins the eye and the ear?
While it should have been stated that this very [Self], characterized in such a way, employs the ear and the other senses, is this reply, "the ear of the ear," not inconsistent?

This is no fault, because its specific nature cannot be understood otherwise. For if it were characterized by its own distinct activity separate from the activities of the ear and the other senses, [then this description would be appropriate].

One might understand [the self] as the director of the ear and other organs, like a user of a sickle or similar tools; however, this would be an inappropriate reply. For here, a director of the ear and other organs—distinguished by its own specific activity—is not apprehended in the manner of one who wields a sickle or the like. Rather, it is understood through the activity of the ear and other organs themselves when they are combined, characterized by perception, volition, and determination, and evidenced by the resulting fruit: namely, that there exists a non-composite entity, impelled by whose purpose the collection of the ear and other organs functions, just like a house or similar structures.

Because composite things exist for the sake of another, it is understood that there is an operator of the ear and so forth; therefore, this reply, "the hearing of the hearing," and so on, is entirely appropriate.

But what is the meaning of the phrase "the hearing of the hearing" and so forth here? For in this case, there is no purpose served by one hearing for another hearing, just as there is no need for one light for another light.

This is not a fault. The meaning of the words here is as follows: the ear is indeed observed to be capable of manifesting its own object; however, that capacity of the ear to manifest its own object exists only when there is the eternal, indivisible, and all-pervading light of the Self within consciousness, and not when it is absent. Therefore, the expression "the ear of the ear," and so forth, is logically justified. And likewise, other scriptural passages state: "By the light of the Self alone, he sits."

"Thereby all this shines," "By whose splendor the sun burns, kindled with heat," and so forth; and in the *Gītā*: "The light residing in the sun which illuminates the entire world," and "Likewise, O Bhārata, the Knower of the Field illumines the whole field. And in the *Kaṭhaka*: "The eternal among the non-eternal, the consciousness among conscious beings. It is well known that it is precisely the ear and other senses that are the conscious self of everything; however, that is here set aside, for there exists something accessible to the intellect of the wise, the innermost of all, immovable, unborn, undecaying, immortal, and fearless.
The reply that "the ear and so forth are themselves the ear and so forth, being the cause of their respective capacities," as well as the meaning of the word [in the text], is indeed appropriate.

Likewise, for the mind—that is, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—it is the "mind. For without the internal organ, the light of consciousness would not be capable of the functions of volition and determination regarding its own objects. Therefore, even for the mind, it is called "mind. Here, the term "mind" is used by identifying intellect (buddhi) and mind (manas) as one.

Or rather: "That which [is] the speech of speech. The word *yat* (which) has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*) and is connected with all [the senses], beginning with the ear—that is, because [it is] the hearing of the ear, because [it is] the mind of the mind, and so forth. The accusative case in *vāco ha vācam* is changed into the nominative, as seen in the expression *prāṇasya prāṇaḥ*. Why is the accusative not maintained in *prāṇasya prāṇam* to conform to *vāco ha vācam*? Because it is more appropriate to conform to the majority.
Regarding the word "vācam," one should have said simply "vāk" in accordance with the two words "sa u prāṇasya prāṇaḥ"; for in this way, the agreement of the majority would have been maintained.

It is proper to indicate by the nominative case alone that which has been asked about. That which was asked by you—the "breath of breath," meaning the specific function of breath known as *prāṇa*—is because the power of breathing belongs to that [Self]. For breathing is not possible for that which is not presided over by the Self, according to such scriptural passages as: "Who indeed would inhale? Who would exhale? If this bliss did not exist in this space? and "He leads the *prāṇa* upward and casts the *apāna* downward," etc. Furthermore, it will be stated here later on: "Know that very thing by which the *prāṇa* is led forth to be Brahman."
In the context of the sense organs beginning with the ear, it would have been more appropriate to mention the nose (*ghrāṇa*) rather than the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

This is true; however, the Śruti considers that by the very mention of *prāṇa*, the nose is already included. What is intended here as the meaning of the section is that which is the purpose for which the entire collection of instruments functions—that is, Brahman.

Likewise, regarding the eye, which illuminates form: the capacity of the eye to perceive form belongs only to it when it is presided over by the consciousness of the Self. Therefore, [it says] "the eye of the eye."

Since the questioner desires to know the meaning of what was asked, the word "having known" (*jñātvā*) is to be supplied [to the text] regarding the ear and so forth, which have been described as having the characteristics of the ear and so on, as stated in the Brāhmaṇa. This is also because of the scriptural statement of the result, "they become immortal" (*amṛtā bhavanti*); for immortality is attained through knowledge, as is evident from the force of the statement, "having known, one is liberated. Having abandoned the entire collection of bases such as the ear—that is, having formed the notion of "self" with respect to the ear and so forth—one, being conditioned by those [senses], is born, dies, and transmigrates by way of their nature.

Therefore, having understood that the Brahman-Self is characterized as the ear and so forth, and having transcended—that is, having abandoned—the state of being the ear and so forth (which is possible to abandon), they become immortal, possessing the nature of immortality. This means: having departed from this world—turning away from the worldly conduct characterized by the notions of "mine" and "I" toward sons, friends, wives, and kinsmen—and having become one who has renounced all desires. Thus they become immortal.

"Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22); "The Self-existent pierced the openings [of the senses] outward; therefore one looks outward, not at the inner self. But some wise man, desiring immortality, looked within himself with his vision turned back" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.4.1); and "When all the desires that dwell in his heart are cast away... then he attains Brahman here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.7). From such scriptural passages as these, or else, because the abandonment of desire is already established by the very word "having transcended" (atimucya), the meaning is: having departed from this world, having passed away from this body, that is, having died. ||2||
Since Brahman is the very self of the ear and the other senses, therefore:

"The eye does not go there, nor speech, nor mind; we do not know it, nor do we understand how one should instruct it. It is indeed other than the known, and furthermore, it is above the unknown. Thus have we heard from those of old who explained it to us. (3)

The eye does not go there, O Takshin Brāhmaṇī, because it is impossible for something to act upon itself. Likewise, speech does not go there. For when a sound is uttered by speech, it reveals its object; at that time, it is said that "speech goes toward the object. But the Self (ātman) is the essence of both that sound and the instrument that produces it; therefore, speech does not go there. Just as fire, though it is both a burner and an illuminator, does not illuminate or burn itself, so it is in this case.

The mind is not the mind of another; although it exists as that which conceives and determines, it does not conceive or determine itself, for its own nature is Brahman. Indeed, the cognition of an object arises through the senses and the mind; because that [Brahman] is beyond their scope, we do not know that Brahman as being "like this."

Therefore, we do not know how—that is, in what manner—one might instruct or teach this Brahman to a disciple; such is the intended meaning. For that which falls within the range of the senses can be taught to another by means of qualifiers such as genus, quality, and action. But Brahman does not possess such qualifiers as genus and so forth; therefore, it is difficult to make it understood to disciples through instruction. Thus, [the author] shows that great effort must be exerted both in the teaching and in the comprehension of its meaning.

"We do not know, nor do we understand how this might be taught"—when such an absolute rejection of the method of instruction has been reached, this exception is stated. It is true that the Supreme cannot be made known by means of direct perception and other such instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); however, it can indeed be made known through scripture (*āgama*). Therefore, for the purpose of instructing upon That, He declares the scripture:

"It is indeed other than the known, and also other than the unknown. It is indeed other, it is distinct from that which was introduced as the "hearer of hearing" and so forth for the ears and other senses, and which is beyond their range. For it is certainly other than the known. What is called "known" is that which has been reached through the act of knowing (*vidi-kriyā*) with intensity—that is, something somewhere known by someone as an object of the act of knowing. Everything that is manifested is indeed known; therefore, the meaning is that it is other than that.

When the objection arises that [Brahman] is thus unknown or unperceived, he says: "Moreover (atho), even from the unknown"—that is, from the opposite of the known, characterized as the undifferentiated (avyākṛta) ignorance which is the seed of differentiation—"above" (adhi)—the word "above" being used here in the sense of "distinctly" (lakṣaṇayā) meaning "other. For it is well known that whatever exists above something else is distinct from it.

That which is known is small, mortal, and of the nature of suffering; therefore, it is to be abandoned. When it is said, "The Brahman is other than the known," its non-abandonability is thereby stated. Likewise, when it is said, "Beyond the unknown," its non-acceptability is stated. For a cause is accepted as something distinct from its effect by one who seeks that effect. Consequently, nothing other than the Knower can be accepted for any other purpose.

Thus, by negating both the knowable and the unknowable as being other [than the Self], the inquiry of the disciple regarding Brahman as an object is brought to an end, because [Brahman] is non-different from one's own Self. For it is not possible for any entity other than one's own Self to exist as something distinct from the known and the unknown; therefore, "the Self is Brahman"—this is the meaning of the sentence. This is also confirmed by other scriptural passages such as, "This Self is Brahman," "The Self which is free from evil," "That Brahman which is immediate and direct," and "The Self which is within all."

Thus, he states that this meaning of the Vedic statement—which establishes Brahman as the Self of all, devoid of all distinctions, and the light of pure consciousness—has been attained through the lineage of the teacher’s instruction, beginning with the words "Thus have we heard," and so forth. Brahman must be understood precisely through the lineage of the teacher’s instruction, and not through logic, nor through eloquence, intelligence, extensive learning, austerity, sacrifice, and the like; thus, "Thus have we heard" means that we have heard the word of our predecessors, the teachers.
The meaning is: those teachers who have explained, that is, have clearly narrated, the Veda to us, to ourselves.

When the statement, "It is indeed other than the known, and furthermore, above the unknown," establishes that the Self is Brahman, a doubt arises in the listener: "How indeed can the Self be Brahman? For the so-called 'Self' is one who is engaged in ritual action and meditation, a transmigrating being who desires to attain the gods such as Brahmā or heaven by performing the means of ritual action or meditation. Therefore, it must be something else—Viṣṇu, Īśvara, Indra, or Prāṇa—that is worthy of worship as Brahman, but not the Self; for this would contradict common worldly understanding."

Just as other logicians declare that the Self is distinct from Īśvara, so too do those devoted to ritual action worship entirely different deities, saying, "Sacrifice to this one; sacrifice to that one. Therefore, it is logical that what is known and worthy of worship should be the Brahman, while the one who worships is something other than it. Perceiving this doubt through the student's outward signs, or from his words, [the Teacher] said: "Do not suspect it thus: That which is not expressed by speech, but by which speech is expressed—that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. (4)

That which has existence as pure consciousness alone—the organ of speech (*vāk*), so-called "speech," which is of the nature of fire (*āgneya*) and is attached to the eight locations such as the root of the tongue and others, serving as the instrument that manifests phonemes (*varṇa*); and the phonemes themselves, which are delimited by convention regarding meaning, being just this many and employed in such a sequence—this word (*śabda*) manifested by them, consisting of a *pada*, is called "speech" (*vāk*). This is according to the Vedic revelation: "The letter *a* is indeed all speech; it becomes manifold in form, being manifested by the *sparśa*, *antastha*, and *ūṣman* [classes of consonants]."

Measured and unmeasured, tone, truth and falsehood—these are the modifications (*vikāra*) of that Speech which is delimited by words and possesses the qualities of the organs of speech. That Brahman by which the speech, together with its instruments, is raised up—that is, manifested, expressed, and employed—and by the light of consciousness (*caitanya-jyotis*) it shines forth; this is that which is called "Speech" (*vāk*). As it is said in the *Vājasaneyaka*: "He who speaks is speech," and "He who, from within, controls speech," and so forth.

Having raised the question, "That speech which is in men is established in sounds; does some Brāhmaṇa know it?", the answer is stated: "That speech is that by which one speaks in a dream. For that speech of the speaker is eternal, having the nature of the light of consciousness, according to the Vedic scripture: "Indeed, there is no loss of the speaker's speech."

Know that very nature of the Self as Brahman—the unsurpassed, called the Infinite (bhūman), and "Brahman" because of its vastness. Set aside those limiting adjuncts such as speech and so forth, through which conventional designations proceed—such as "the speech of speech," "the eye of the eye," "the ear of the ear," "the mind of the mind," "the agent," "the enjoyer," "the knower," "the controller," "the ruler," "consciousness," "bliss," and "Brahman"—and realize the Self alone as the undifferentiated. This is in the Supreme, the Non-conventional, the Indifferentiated, and the Absolute Equality of Brahman.

"Know that alone to be Brahman"—this is the meaning of the word "eva" (alone). One should not meditate upon or contemplate as Brahman that which is qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as the non-Self, the Lord, and so forth, thinking, "This which is here is Brahman. Even though it has been stated, "Know that alone to be Brahman," the fact that the non-Self is not Brahman is stated again in the phrase "this [which is here] is not Brahman," either for the sake of emphasis (*niyamārtha*) or to exclude the notion of anything else being Brahman (*anyabrahmabuddhiparisaṃkhyānārtha*). ||4||
That which the mind does not perceive, that by which they say the mind is perceived—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship. 5.

"That which one does not perceive with the mind"—here, "mind" (*manas*) refers to the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), as intellect (*buddhi*) and mind are grasped as one. It is called "mind" because one perceives by means of it; it is common to all the instruments of cognition (*karaṇa*) because it pervades all objects. According to the Śruti: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, shame, intelligence—all this is indeed the mind," the mind possesses the modifications (*vṛtti*) such as desire and so forth.

The world does not perceive that consciousness-light which is the illuminator of the mind, nor does it will or resolve through it; because the mind is its illuminator and controller, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) does not operate toward itself as being "just within" with respect to all objects. For it is only when the mind is illumined by the consciousness-light residing within that it possesses the capacity for thinking.

Therefore, those who know the Brahman say that the mind, together with its conduct, has been made the object of the Brahman and is pervaded by it; they declare this. Therefore, know that very mind to be the Self, the inward perceiver, the Brahman. "Not this," and so forth, is as explained before. (5)
That which one does not see with the eye, by that one sees the eyes; know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people here worship.

That which the world does not see and does not take as an object with the eye joined to the modifications of the internal organ—that by which the eyes, which are differentiated by the various modifications of the internal organ, see; that by which the visual modification perceives, makes an object of, and pervades through the light of the consciousness-self—that alone [is the eye], and so forth, as explained previously. ||6||
That which one does not hear with the ear, by which this very ear is heard—that alone know thou to be Brahman, and not that which people here worship. 7.

That which the world does not hear with the ear—which is presided over by the deity of the quarters, is an effect of space, and is joined with a modification of the mind—and that by which this ear is heard, which is made an object by the light of the Self that is consciousness; that indeed [is Brahman], and so forth, as before. ||7||
That by which one breathes through the vital breath (prāṇa), and by which the vital breath itself is led forth—that alone know thou to be Brahman; this [world] which they worship is not that. || 8 ||

That which one does not smell—that is, that which one does not make into an object of perception as a fragrance—by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), i.e., the sense of smell (*ghrāṇa*) situated within the nostrils together with the functions of the internal organ and the vital air; and that by which the vital breath is led toward its own objects through being illumined by the light of the conscious Self—all this is the same [as previously explained]. ||8||
Thus ends the first section. || 1 ||

Thus, having been made to understand that the Self is Brahman—which is the opposite of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—the teacher says "If... and so forth, in order to shake the student's understanding, lest the student grasp it with the thought, "I am indeed Brahman; I know this well. [The student might think:
"But surely, the firm conviction 'I know [Brahman] well' is precisely what is desired."

True; the realization is indeed desired and certain, for [the text says], "I do not know [it] well. For whatever object is to be known becomes an objective field, that can be well-known, just as fire can burn wood, but not its own nature. Indeed, the well-ascertained meaning of all the Vedāntas is that the Self of every knower is Brahman. And here, that very point has been established through the dialogue of question and answer beginning with, "The hearer of the hearer."

Furthermore, it has been specifically determined by the statement, "That which is not expressed by speech. The certainty of the tradition of those who know the Veda is stated in the words, "It is indeed other than the known, and likewise above the unknown. Having introduced this, he will conclude with, "It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for the teacher to dispel the student's notion that he knows well.

For the knower cannot be known by the knower, just as fire cannot be burned by fire. Nor is there another knower of Brahman who could have something else as an object of knowledge; for [the scripture] says, "There is no other knower than this," thereby negating any other cognizer. Therefore, the conviction that "I know Brahman well" is indeed false. Thus, the Teacher’s statement beginning with "If... is entirely appropriate.

If you think, "I know it well," then surely what you know of the form of Brahman is very small—both that which you know of it and that which is among the gods. Therefore, I believe that what remains to be pondered by you is indeed yet to be known.

If you should ever think, "I know it well," or "I know the Veda thoroughly"—anticipating that even though [the Veda] is difficult to comprehend as it has been heard, some of excellent intellect whose defects have been eliminated might grasp it while others might not—he says "yadi" (if) and so forth, expressing doubt.

And it has been observed that when Prajāpati said, "This person who is seen in the eye—this is the Self; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is Brahman," the Asura king Virocana, though wise, understood the opposite meaning—the body as the Self—even though it was logically untenable, due to the influence of his inherent defect. Similarly, Indra, the king of the gods, failing to understand even after it was stated once, twice, and thrice, attained the very first teaching regarding Brahman upon the fourth occasion, depending on the exhaustion of his inherent defect.

Even in the world, among those listening to a single teacher, one understands correctly, another incorrectly, another wrongly, and another does not understand at all. What then need be said regarding the reality of the Self, which transcends the senses? For here, all the dialecticians who argue for existence or non-existence are in disagreement. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for the Teacher to speak with apprehension, saying, "Even though it has been stated with perfect certainty as 'the Brahman that is known,'" because of the difficulty of its comprehension, [adding] "if you think... and so forth. You surely know only the small, limited form of Brahman.

Are there many forms of Brahman—both great and small—by reason of which [the scripture] says, "only the small," and so forth? Certainly; for the many forms of Brahman are produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of name and form, not by its own nature. By its own nature, however, forms along with sound and the other qualities are denied, as it is said: "That which is without sound, without touch, without form, imperishable, and likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell."

[Objection: Is it not the case that whatever property by which something is defined is its very own nature (*svarūpa*)? Thus, that specific quality by which Brahman is defined would itself be its nature. To this it is replied: Consciousness (*caitanya*) is not a property belonging to earth or any other [element], nor to any of them in their transformed states; rather, it is the form of Brahman. Brahman is defined by consciousness. And so it has been stated in the Śrutis regarding the form of Brahman: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (*vijñānam ānandam brahma*), "It is indeed a mass of consciousness" (*vijñānaghana eva*), "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite" (*satyam jñānam anantam brahma*), and "Brahman is pure intelligence" (*prajñānam brahma*). Thus, the form of Brahman is specified in the scriptures.

This is true; nevertheless, it is designated by words such as "consciousness" (vijñāna) and so forth only through the medium of the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the internal organ, body, and senses, because it conforms to them—due to the growth, contraction, cutting, and destruction of the body and so forth—but not in itself. As for its own nature, it will remain as it is established in the teaching: "It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know."

The phrase "that which is the form of this Brahman" is to be connected with what precedes. You do not know merely that small form of this Brahman as delimited by the internal adjunct (*adhyātma-upādhi*); even that form of this Brahman as delimited by the divine adjunct (*adhidaivata-upādhi*) which you know among the gods—that too, I believe, you surely know only as something small. Whether it be within the self or among the gods, because it is delimited by an adjunct, its smallness does not cease.

The intention is that the Brahman—which is devoid of all distinctions of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), peaceful, infinite, one, non-dual, called the "Fullness" (*bhūman*), and eternal—is not something easily understood.

Since this is so, therefore, I think that even now your Brahman must still be investigated and deliberated upon by you. Thus addressed by the teacher, the disciple sat down in a secluded place and, being composed, reflected upon the meaning of the scripture as taught by the teacher; having determined it through reasoning and attained personal realization, he approached the teacher and said: "Now, at last, I consider the Brahman to be known. ||1||
How so? Listen:
"I do not think 'I know well,' nor do I think 'I do not know'; yet I know. That which we know, he knows; that which we do not know, he does not know, yet he knows. (2)

"I do not think 'I know well,' nor do I think 'I know Brahman well. Then, when it was asked, 'In that case, Brahman is not known by you,' he replied: 'No, it is not that I do not know; I know it. By the word 'and' (ca) in 'I know it,' it is meant that he both knows and does not know."

Is this not a contradiction? "I do not think 'I know well,' nor do I think 'I do not know'; yet I know. If you do not think "I know well," how can you think "I know"? Or if you think "I indeed know," how can you not think "I know well"? It is a contradiction—apart from doubt and error—that by the very same means through which a thing is known, that same thing is not known well.
Nor can it be determined that the Veda is to be known as being characterized by doubt or by error; for doubt and error are everywhere well known precisely as causes of harm.

Even though he was thus being challenged by the teacher, the disciple did not waver, due to the power of the traditional transmission of the scripture spoken by the teacher—namely, "That is indeed other than the known, and moreover above the unknown"—and due to the power of reasoning and personal experience. And he roared, demonstrating his own firm certainty regarding the knowledge of Brahman. How so? It is said: whoever among us, those who practice together with us in the study of the Veda, knows that word spoken by me according to its true reality, he indeed knows That.

What, then, is that statement? To this he says: "Neither does one know it, nor does one not know it. That very reality which was described by the words, "It is indeed other than the known, and moreover, above the unknown," has been ascertained by joining it with inference and experience, and expressed in another sentence as "Neither does one know it, nor does one not know it. This was said for the purpose of harmonizing with the teacher's understanding and for the purpose of removing the misconceptions of those of dull intellect. Thus, the proclamation, "He who knows that among us knows it," becomes logically consistent. ||2||

Having desisted from the dialogue between disciple and teacher, the Śruti reveals the very meaning established by that entire conversation in its own form, beginning with the words "He by whom it is not thought... (Yasyāmatam...): "He by whom it is not thought, by him it is thought; he who knows it not, he knows it. It is unknown to those who know, and known to those who do not know. (3)

He whose thought regarding Brahman is unthought, unknown, and not perceived—that is, he whose opinion, intention, and resolve is that "Brahman is [inexpressible]," his thought is known; his intention is correctly that "Brahman is [beyond conceptualization]. But he whose thought, knowledge, and perception is that "I have known Brahman"—that is, he whose resolve is so—he indeed does not know; he does not truly understand Brahman.

He determines the two positions stated for the learned and the ignorant: "The unknown is [the Brahman] of those who know. This means that the Brahman is "unknown"—that is, unperceived and indeed not known—by those who know, by those who have correctly understood it. "The known is [the Brahman] of those who do not know" means of those who lack right vision, whose sense organs, mind, and intellect perceive the Self only within them; it does not refer to those whose intellects are entirely unrefined. For such people do not even have the thought, "The Brahman has been known by us."

However, for those who perceive the Self in the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of the senses, mind, and intellect, because they do not perceive the distinction from the limiting adjunct of Brahman, and because the adjuncts such as the intellect are themselves known, the notion that "Brahman is known" arises as an error; therefore, this incorrect view is presented as the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) in the words, "by those who do not know what is known. Alternatively, the latter half of the verse beginning with "the unknown" serves to state the reason [for the error]. ||3||

"It is unknown to those who know"—this has been determined. If the Brahman were absolutely unknown, then no distinction would arise between worldly people and those who know the Brahman. Furthermore, "unknown to those who know" is a mutual contradiction. To explain how that Brahman becomes rightly known, he says: "It is held to be known through awakening; for through that one finds immortality. Through the Self one finds strength; through knowledge one finds immortality. (4)

"Known by the awakened one, awakened at every awakening. By the word "awakening" (bodha), the mental modifications (bauddhāḥ pratyayāḥ) are meant. That Self, to which all modifications become objects, awakens with respect to all awakenings. The witness of all modifications, whose nature is solely the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is characterized through the modifications themselves as being non-different from them within the modifications; there is no other means for the realization of the Inner Self.

Therefore, when Brahman is known as the inner self of all cognitions, then that is considered the right vision (*samyagdarśana*); this is the meaning. Furthermore, if it is seen in all cognitions, then its nature as the seer—which is devoid of arising and passing away, its eternity, its pure nature, its selfhood, and its undifferentiated oneness—becomes established in all beings, because there is no difference in its defining characteristic, just as the space within a jar, a mountain, or a cave is one with the universal space.

Thus, the meaning of the scriptural statement that Brahman is "other than the known and the unknown" becomes perfectly established. For another Vedic text says: "The seer of seeing, the hearer of hearing, the thinker of thinking, the knower of knowing."

Furthermore, if it is explained that "known by the act of knowing" (*pratibodhaviditam*) means one knows the agent of the act of knowing by means of the characteristic of the act of knowing—that is, by the characteristic of cognition—just as one says "the wind is that which moves the branches of the tree," then the Self would be a substance possessing the power of the act of knowing, rather than being of the very nature of cognition itself. In that case, cognition would arise and perish; and when cognition arises, the Self would be characterized by that specific act of knowing.

When consciousness perishes, that which has lost its consciousness becomes a mere substance, devoid of distinction. This being the case, defects such as being subject to modification, having parts, being non-eternal, and being impure cannot be avoided.

Furthermore, even according to the followers of Kaṇāda, who hold that cognition produced by the conjunction of the self and the mind inheres in the self—and that therefore the self possesses the quality of being a cognizer, yet the self is not of the nature of modification, but is merely a substance like a jar which is the locus of color—in this view as well, the Brahman would be an insentient mere substance. Consequently, such scriptural passages as "Brahman is consciousness and bliss," and "Brahman is pure intelligence," would be contradicted.

Because the self is partless and lacks spatial divisions, and because the mind is eternally conjoined with it, the impossibility of a fixed rule for the arising of memory would be unavoidable. Furthermore, the attribution of the quality of association to the self would be a mere fabrication, contrary to Śruti, Smṛti, and reason. For the Śruti and Smṛti declare: "Unattached, for it does not cling," and "Unattached, yet supporting all. And the reasoning is this: that which possesses qualities associates with that which possesses qualities, not with that which is of a different genus.

Therefore, it would be contrary to reason to claim that the Nirguṇa (devoid of qualities), Nirviśeṣa (without distinctions), and Sarvavilakṣaṇa (distinct from everything)—which is of a nature unequal to anything else—is created by something else. Consequently, the meaning that the Self is the Brahman whose nature is the light of eternal and undiminished consciousness is established only through the Self’s being the knower of all cognitions, and not otherwise. Therefore, the statement "that which is known through self-awakening is the realized truth" is to be understood exactly in the sense we have explained.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of the statement "known through self-awareness" (*pratibodhavidita*), it is explained as follows: when the Self (*ātman*) is characterized by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*), one conceptually constructs a distinction based on the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) as an adjunct, and thus employs the conventional expression that "the Self knows itself"—as in "one sees the Self in the Self alone" and "O Supreme Person, you know yourself by yourself through yourself. However, in the case of the Self that is devoid of adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), where there is absolute unity, neither self-awareness nor awareness by another is possible.

Because its very nature is consciousness, it cannot depend upon another consciousness, just as light does not require another light. On the Buddhist position, however, if consciousness were self-cognized, it would follow that consciousness is momentary and devoid of a self (nirātman), which would contradict such scriptural passages as: "For there is no loss of the knower's knowledge, because of its imperishability"; "Eternal, omnipresent, and all-pervading"; and "This indeed is the great, unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal, and fearless. Thus, these and other Śruti texts would be subverted.

Furthermore, as for those who imagine that by the word "awakening" (pratibodha) is meant an awakening without an object, such as the awakening of one who has slept; or others who say that awakening is knowledge occurring all at once—whether it be without an object or with an object, whether occurring once or repeatedly, it is indeed simply awakening.

The meaning is this: because one attains—that is, obtains—immortality, which is the state of not dying, the abiding in one's own Self, namely liberation, from the aforementioned awakening (pratibodha), which consists in the knowledge of the Self through awakening; therefore, that which is known through awakening alone is considered [the means]. For it is held that the fact that awakening has the innermost Self (pratyagātman) as its object is the cause of immortality. Indeed, the state of non-immortality does not belong to the Self when it is perceived as non-Self. Since the Self is the Self, its immortality is indeed without cause; likewise, the mortality of the Self arises from the realization of non-Selfhood through ignorance (avidyā).

But how does one find immortality through the aforementioned knowledge of the Self? To this he says: "By the Self"—that is, by its own nature—one finds or obtains *vīrya*, meaning power, strength, or capacity. The power produced by wealth, allies, mantras, herbs, austerity, or yoga is unable to overcome death, because it is produced by impermanent things; however, the power produced by the knowledge of the Self one finds by the Self alone and not by anything else. Therefore, since the power of the knowledge of the Self has no other means [for its realization], that very power is able to overcome death.

Since one finds this vigor produced by the knowledge of the Self through the Self alone, therefore, by means of that knowledge concerning the Self, one finds immortality—that is, the state of being immortal. As it is said in the Atharva Veda: "This Self is not to be attained by one who is devoid of strength. Thus, the reason is established: for one indeed finds immortality. ||4||

Alas, miserable indeed is the attainment of birth, old age, death, disease, and so forth, due to ignorance, among the multitudes of living beings in saṃsāra—abounding in suffering such as those of gods, humans, animals, and pretas.

Therefore: "If one has realized [the Self] here, then there is truth; if one has not realized it here, there is great ruin. Having searched for it among every single being, the wise, after departing from this world, become immortal. (5)

If a human being here, being qualified and capable, should have known the Self as described by its characteristics—having realized it in the manner stated—then indeed there exists truth, non-destruction, purposefulness, existence, or ultimate reality in this human birth. "If he did not know here"—if the living being, though qualified, did not know; then there is a great, long-lasting, and infinite ruin, a destruction characterized by the continuity of birth, old age, death, and so forth, which is the course of saṃsāra.

Therefore, the wise Brāhmaṇas, discerning merit and defect in this way, having discovered, known, and directly realized the single reality of the Self (ātmatattva)—the Brāhma—within all beings, both stationary and moving; having departed, that is, having turned away from this world characterized by ignorance in the form of the notions of "mine" and "I"; and having attained the non-dual state of being the Self of all, they become immortal, meaning they become the Brāhma itself.
This is according to the Vedic scripture: "He who knows that supreme Brāhma becomes the Brāhma itself. ||5||

In the third section, because of such scriptural declarations as, "The unknown is known to those who know, and the known is unknown to those who do not know," it is observed that whatever exists is "known" through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while that which does not exist is "unknown," like the horn of a hare, being absolutely non-existent. Thus, lest there arise the delusion among those of dull intellect that this Brahman is non-existent simply because it is unknown, this narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) is commenced for that purpose.

For that very Brahman is the ruler in every respect, the supreme deity even among the gods, the supreme Lord even among the lords, difficult to comprehend, the cause of victory for the gods, and the cause of defeat for the Asuras; how then could it not exist? Thus, subsequent statements are seen to be consistent with this meaning. Alternatively, [these passages serve] as praise for the knowledge of Brahman. How so? For through the knowledge of Brahman, the gods beginning with Agni attained preeminence among the gods, and Indra attained a state even more exalted than theirs.

Alternatively, this narrative is intended to show that the Brahman is difficult to comprehend—for even Agni and the others, despite their extreme brilliance, understood the Brahman only with great difficulty, and likewise Indra, though he was the lord of the gods.

Or, the entire story may be directed toward the injunction for the Upaniṣad to be taught hereafter; or rather, it is for the purpose of demonstrating that the egoistic conceit of living beings regarding agency, enjoyership, and so forth, apart from the knowledge of Brahman, is false—just as the gods had a conceit regarding victory and the like.
"Verily, the Brahman won a victory for the gods; in that victory of the Brahman, the gods exulted. (1)

The *brāhmaṇa*, indeed, possessing the characteristics as described, won a supreme victory for the sake of the gods; having conquered the Asuras in the battle between the gods and the Asuras—those enemies of the world who were destroyers of the divine bridge—he bestowed upon the gods that victory and its fruit for the stability of the universe. In that victory of the *brāhmaṇa*, the gods, Agni and the others, were truly magnified, having attained greatness. ||1||

Then, not knowing that this victory and this greatness belonged to the Lord—the Self abiding within, the innermost Self, the omniscient, the ordainer of the fruits of all actions for living beings, the omnipotent one desiring to maintain the world—they thought: "This victory is ours alone; this greatness is ours alone. He knew what was in their hearts and appeared before them; they did not recognize him and asked, "What is this spirit? (2)

Those gods reflected—they perceived—that "this victory is ours alone, brought about by our own selves as limited by the forms of Agni and the others; this majesty, characterized by the states of being Agni, Vāyu, Indra, and so forth, which is the fruit of victory, is experienced by us; it was not brought about by the Lord who is our innermost Self. To those who thus possessed such false conceit, the Veda (Brahman) indeed became aware of that false perception of theirs. For He is the Seer of all, because He is the impeller of the organs of all beings.

Having perceived the false knowledge of the gods, [the Lord] thought: "Lest the gods, like the Asuras, should suffer defeat due to false pride, I shall favor them by removing their false pride out of compassion for them. For the sake of those gods, he indeed manifested himself in a form created by the majesty of his own yoga—a form that was not excessively wonderful yet capable of causing amazement—and appeared within the range of the senses of the gods;
he appeared as it were. The gods did not recognize that manifested being of Brahmā; they did not understand at all: "What is this? Is it a Yakṣa, a great venerable being? ||2||
They said to Agni Jātavedas, "Find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied.

Not knowing that, those gods, filled with internal fear and desiring to understand it, spoke to Agni Jātavedas—who was at their head and nearly omniscient—saying: "O Jātavedas, find out this Yakṣa standing within our range; discern it specifically for us: what kind of radiant being is this Yakṣa? ||3||
He ran toward him; he addressed him, saying, "Who are you? He replied, "I am Agni," or "I am Jātavedas. ||4||

"So be it," [the Yakṣa said], and he ran toward that Yakṣa; Agni went toward it. When Agni had approached and was about to question it, but remained silent out of diffidence in its presence, that Yakṣa addressed him, saying, "O Agni, who are you? Thus questioned by the Brāhmaṇa, Agni replied: "I am Agni"—meaning he is well-known by the name Agni—and "Jātavedas," praising himself by means of these two well-known names. ||4||
"What power do you have against him? I could burn all this that is on the earth. ||5||

To him who had spoken thus, the Brahmin said: "What is the power and capability in you who are so renowned for your virtues and name? He replied: "I could burn this entire world, I could reduce to ashes everything here on earth, including the stationary things. The phrase "on earth" is used as an illustration, because even that which stands in the intermediate space is indeed burned by fire. ||5||

He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Burn this! It approached with all its speed, but it was unable to burn it; it turned back from that very spot, for it did not succeed in discerning what this yakṣa was. ||6||

To him who was thus possessed of such pride, the Brahmin placed a blade of grass before the fire. He said, "Burn even this much—a mere blade of grass—in my presence; if you are capable of burning it, then abandon your pride as a burner everywhere. Thus addressed, he rushed toward that grass, having gone near the grass with all his speed—that is, with a velocity produced by every effort. Having gone there, he was not able, nor did he succeed, in burning it.

Being unable to burn that blade of grass, Jātavedas (Fire), ashamed and his promise frustrated, returned silently from that very Yakṣa toward the gods; having turned back, he went away, saying, "I was not able—I could not—specifically to discern this Yakṣa, as to what this Yakṣa is. ||6||
Then they said to Vāyu, "Vāyu, find out what this Yakṣa is. He replied, "So be it. ||7||
He ran toward him; he addressed him, saying, "Who are you? He replied, "I am indeed Vāyu," or "I am Mātariśvan. ||8||
"What power do you possess? he asked. "I would take all this away from you, even if it were on this earth," [he replied]. ||9||

He placed a blade of grass before him, saying, "Take this! He ran toward it with all his speed, but he was unable to take it; he turned back from that very spot, saying, "I am not able to discern what this Yakṣa is. ||10||

Immediately after that, they spoke to Vāyu: "O Vāyu, find out this," and so forth; the meaning is the same as before. He is called Vāyu because he moves (*vāti*), or because he restrains (*damayati*) and binds (*dadhāti*). He is Mātariśvan because he swells (*śvayati*) in the mother (*mātari*), namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "I might take up all this, whatever is here on earth," and so forth, is exactly the same [as the previous passage]. (7–10)
Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, find out what this Yakṣa is. "So be it," he replied, and he ran toward it; then it vanished from him. ||11||

Then they said to Indra, "O Maghavan, understand this," and so forth, as in the previous section. Indra is the Supreme Lord; he is called Maghavan because of his power. Saying "So be it," he rushed toward it. As Indra approached its vicinity, that Brahman vanished from sight. Because Indra’s pride regarding his own status as Indra had to be utterly dispelled, the Brahman did not grant even a word of reply to Indra. ||11||
In that very space, he beheld a woman of great beauty approaching—Umā, the daughter of Himavat—and said to her, "What is this yakṣa? ||12||

In that very same space, in that region of the sky where the Yakṣa had manifested itself and then vanished, and where Indra himself was at the time of its disappearance, Indra remained in that very space, reflecting, "What is that Yakṣa?"; he did not turn back, as Agni and the others had done.

Perceiving that Indra had devotion toward the Yakṣa, the Vidyā appeared in the form of a woman, assuming the likeness of Umā. Indra [beheld] that Umā, who was exceedingly beautiful—indeed, Vidyā is the most beautiful of all beautiful things; thus, the epithet "exceedingly beautiful" (bahuśobhamānā) is appropriate here, meaning she was shining intensely like Haimavatī, as if adorned with ornaments made of gold—or alternatively, Umā herself is called Haimavatī because she is the daughter of Himavat and always dwells together with the omniscient Lord.
Thinking that she was capable of knowing it, Indra approached Umā and indeed spoke to her, asking: "Tell me, what is this yakṣa who vanished after showing himself? ||12||
Thus ends the third section. ||3||
"It was Brahman," he said. "It was indeed in the victory of Brahman that you exulted. Then, indeed, he understood: "It was Brahman. ||1||

She said, "It is indeed Brāhmaṇa. For it was by Brāhmaṇa alone, by the Lord alone, that the Asuras were conquered in this victory; you were merely the instrumental cause in that victory of His—therefore, you have become great, you have attained greatness. The word *etad* (this) is used as an adverbial modifier. Your pride, however, is false—the notion that "this victory is ours alone" or "this greatness is ours alone.
From that very statement, Indra understood it to be Brāhmaṇa; because of the emphatic particle *ha eva*, he knew it was from that [Brāhmaṇa] alone, and not through his own independent power. ||1||

Since these gods—Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—have attained proximity to the Brahman through such means as witnessing its conversation, therefore these gods, namely Agni, Vāyu, and Indra, are indeed far more intimate with the Brahman than the other gods; they touched it most closely, and among them, Agni first came to know it as "Brahman. ||2||

Therefore, by their own qualities—namely, their extraordinary power, virtues, and great fortune—these gods surpass, as it were, all other gods; the word "iva" (as it were) is either meaningless or serves to emphasize the sense of certainty.

Agni, Vāyu, and Indra—since these gods, by means of the aforementioned methods such as conversation with the Brāhmaṇa, touched (*pasparśuḥ*) this Brāhmaṇa as the nearest (*nediṣṭham*), the most proximate (*antikamam*), and the dearest (*priyatamam*); and since, for that reason, they, being the first (*prathamaḥ*), meaning the foremost or principal ones, came to know (*vidāñcakāra*) this Brāhmaṇa—this is what is meant by "they came to know. ||2||

Since even Agni and Vāyu learned [the truth] from the very words of Indra—for Indra had first heard it from the words of Umā as "It is Brahman"—therefore Indra indeed surpassed all other gods; he touched it most closely, and he was the first to know that "It is Brahman. ||3||
Therefore, indeed, Indra surpasses the other gods as it were; he touched what was nearest because he was the first to know it—this is the meaning of the sentence beginning with "brahma. ||3||
This is its instruction: "When lightning flashed, ah!"; "When he blinked, ah!"—this is with respect to the divine realm.

This is the instruction (*ādeśa*), that is, the teaching by means of a simile, regarding that aforementioned Brahman. Since Brahman is beyond comparison, this instruction is called an "instruction" because it teaches by means of a point of comparison. What is that? It is that which is well-known in the world as the flashing of lightning—though the expression "as if it had flashed" is figurative, since the actual flashing of lightning is impossible [in the case of Brahman]—this is conceived as "the flashing of lightning. The particle *ā* (here pronounced *ā 3*) signifies a simile; thus the meaning is "like the flashing of lightning," as seen in another Vedic text: "as if it had flashed once. For indeed, like lightning, the Brahman, having shown itself to the gods once, vanished from their sight.

Alternatively, the word "light" (*tejaḥ*) is to be supplied after "of lightning. *Vyadyutat* means "it has flashed"; the sense is that it has flashed like the light of lightning, as if having flashed once. The word *iti* is for the purpose of referring back to the instruction—meaning, "this is the instruction. The word *ca* is for the purpose of conjunction.

And this is another instruction regarding it. What is it? "It closed its eyes," meaning it performed a closing, like the blinking of an eye; the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in the sense of the root itself, and the letter *ā* is for the sake of comparison. The meaning is that it was like the appearance and disappearance of objects before the eye. Thus ends the illustration from the Brāhmaṇa concerning the divine realm, the sphere of the deities. ||4||
Now, with reference to the self: that which moves, as it were, is the mind; and by means of this, one repeatedly recollects this [body], which is volition (saṅkalpa). ||5||

Immediately thereafter, the instruction regarding the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is stated: "That which the mind seems to go toward; that which the intellect (*brahman*) seems to approach and seems to take as its object. And that which the practitioner repeatedly and intensely remembers—that is, brings close to his mind—by means of this mind, is the *saṃkalpa* (volitional thought) of the mind directed toward the *brahman*. For, because the mind has the intellect as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), the *brahman* is manifested through mental states such as volition and memory, appearing as if it were being made an object.
Therefore, this is the instruction concerning the *brahman* with respect to the inner self.

"Like the twinkling of lightning, its nature is one of rapid manifestation with respect to the divine (adhidaivata), and with respect to the self (adhyātma), its nature is manifestation simultaneous with the cognition of the mind"—this is the instruction. For when Brahman is instructed in this manner, it becomes accessible to those of dull intellect; thus, this is the instruction and teaching regarding Brahman. Indeed, Brahman in its unconditioned state cannot be grasped by those of dull intellect. ||5||
Furthermore:
That [forest] is indeed named "That-Forest"; it should be meditated upon as "That-Forest. He who knows this thus—toward him all beings desire to go. 6.

That indeed is called "Tadvana"; that forest (vana) belongs to Him. Because it has become the innermost self (*pratyagātmabhūta*) of that One who has been fully manifested (*praṇijāta*), it is a "forest" (*vana*)—that is, desirable (*vananīya*) and worthy of being resorted to (*saṃbhajanīya*). Therefore, it is named "Tadvana. Since that Brahman is renowned as "Tadvana," for that reason it should be meditated upon and contemplated by means of this very designation of its qualities, namely, "Tadvana."

By this, he states the fruit of the meditation on the name. Whosoever knows—that is, meditates upon—this very Brāhmaṇa as described, endowed with the qualities mentioned, all beings indeed long for him—that is, they desire him—just as they do for the Brāhmaṇa. 6.
Thus instructed, the pupil said to the teacher:
"Sir, tell me the Upanishad. He replied: "I have indeed told you the Upanishad; the Brāhmaṇa itself is your Upanishad. ||7||
"O Venerable Sir, please tell me the Upanishad, that which is to be contemplated, which is the secret.

When the disciple had spoken thus, the teacher said: "The Upanishad has been told—that is, it has been declared—to you. But what is it? He says: "The Brāhmī—the one pertaining to Brahman, the Supreme Self; because the knowledge that transcends [all else] has the Supreme Self as its object—verily (vāva), that alone we have declared to be your Upanishad. By saying "that alone we have declared," he emphasizes that the Upanishad concerning the Supreme Self is precisely what was taught, for the sake of what follows.

What is the intention of the disciple who, having heard the Upaniṣad concerning the Supreme Self, asks, "Sir, please explain the Upaniṣad"? If this question were asked regarding the meaning of what has already been heard, then the question would be redundant and useless, like grinding what is already ground. On the other hand, if the Upaniṣad taught were incomplete, then it would not be appropriate to conclude it with a statement of its fruit, namely, "After departing from this world, they become immortal."

Therefore, even the question regarding the subject matter that remains after the Upaniṣad has been taught is inappropriate, because nothing remains [unexplained]. What, then, is the intention of the questioner? It is said:

Is there an expectation of other means as auxiliaries to the previously taught Upaniṣad by way of being its supplements, or is it independent? If it is dependent, then tell me the Upaniṣad concerning those required objects. If it is independent, then confirm it, saying "There is nothing beyond this," just as Pippalāda did. This is consistent with the teacher’s statement of confirmation: "The Upaniṣad has been told to you."
Is it not the case that this is not a restrictive definition, since he states something else that must be said, namely, "For her, austerity and self-control," and so forth?

True, the teacher speaks of what must be said, but neither as a supplement to the previously mentioned Upaniṣad nor with the intention of referring to other auxiliary means for its realization. Rather, it is with the intention of referring to the means for attaining the knowledge of Brahman (*brāhmī vidyā*), because austerity and the rest are equated [with the Vedas] through their being recited together with the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs (*vedāṅgas*). For it is not possible for the Vedas or their auxiliary limbs, such as phonetics (*śikṣā*) and the rest, to be directly subordinate to the knowledge of Brahman or to serve as its auxiliary means.

If it is argued that even for those things studied together, there should be a distribution and application according to their respective fitness—just as, for instance, the *sūktavāka* and the *anumantraṇa* mantras are divided according to their respective deities—so too might it be postulated that austerity (*tapas*), self-restraint (*dama*), ritual action (*karman*), truthfulness (*satya*), and so forth, are either subsidiary to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) or are auxiliary means to it; and that the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*), by virtue of illuminating their meanings, serve as the means to both ritual action and the knowledge of the Self—thus, this division is appropriate because it is possible and consistent with the connection between the words and their meanings.

No; because it is illogical. This distinction does not apply here. For it is not appropriate for the knowledge of Brahman—which subverts the cognition of all distinctions between actions, factors of action, and results—to have a dependence on anything remaining or a connection with auxiliary means. Furthermore, because the knowledge of Brahman is fixed upon the inner self as its object, which is distinct from all [external] objects, and because its fruit, liberation (*niḥśreyasa*), is such that "one desiring liberation should always abandon action along with its means," [it cannot coexist with ritual activity].

"For that which is to be known must indeed be abandoned; [what remains] for the abandoner is the supreme state, which is inward-facing. Therefore, it is not possible for knowledge to have actions as its auxiliaries or to depend on the remnants of action. Consequently, the distinction [between the two paths] is merely figurative, according to the circumstances, like the *sūktavāka* and the *anumantraṇa* formulas. Thus, it is appropriate that the question and answer are intended for the purpose of definitive determination. This much alone is the Upaniṣad taught for the sake of immortality, independent of anything else. ||7||
For her, austerity, self-control, and ritual action are the foundation; the Vedas are all her limbs; and truth is her abode. ||8||

Therefore, in this life or in many past lives, knowledge arises exactly as it was heard for those who have purified their being through austerity and other means; as stated in the Vedic mantra: "To that great-souled one who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and as to the Divine so to the Guru, these meanings declared here become manifest. And from the Smṛti: "Knowledge arises in men through the destruction of sinful karma."

The word *iti* is intended to indicate that this is illustrative; thus, other factors conducive to the arising of knowledge, such as "humility (*amānitva*), freedom from ostentation (*adambhitva*)" and so forth, which have been previously shown, are also included. "Foundation" refers to the two feet, for when these exist, the knowledge of Brahman is established and proceeds, just as a person stands on his two feet.

The four Vedas and all the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*)—the six beginning with phonetics (*śikṣā*)—constitute the foundation, because the Vedas reveal the knowledge of ritual action and the auxiliaries serve to protect them.

Alternatively, since the word *pratiṣṭhā* (foundation) signifies the metaphorical representation of the feet, the Vedas are the other limbs, such as the head and so forth. In this view, it should be understood that the *Śikṣā* and the other auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*) are already included by the mention of the "Vedas" themselves; for when the possessor of the limbs (*aṅgin*) is grasped, the limbs are necessarily grasped as well, because the limbs are dependent upon him.

Truth is the abode wherein that proximate cause (upaniṣad) resides; that is its abode. "Truth" means the absence of guile and the absence of crookedness in speech, mind, and body. Knowledge takes refuge in those virtuous ones who are free from guile, not among those of demonic nature who are deceitful; for the Śruti says, "In whom there is no crookedness, no falsehood, and no guile. Therefore, truth is conceived as the abode.

The fact that truth (satya), which was already established as a foundation among austerity and the other virtues, is again mentioned here as a "resort" (āyatana) is for the purpose of making known its status as a preeminent means of accomplishment. This is according to the traditional teaching (smṛti): "A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale; truth outweighed the thousand horse-sacrifices. (8)
Whoever knows this thus, having struck away evil, becomes established in the infinite, highest, heavenly world—yes, he becomes established. 9.

He who knows this Brāhma-vidyā—described as "impelled by whom" (*keneṣitam*) and so forth, as previously stated, which is thus highly blessed, praised in the passage beginning with "The Brāhmaṇa [spoke] to the gods," and which is the foundation of all knowledge—he attains immortality; even though this fruit of Brāhma-vidyā has already been mentioned, the text concludes by summarizing it: having struck down evil—that seed of transmigratory existence characterized by ignorance, desire, and action—and having shaken off [all taint], he reaches the infinite, boundless, blissful world of Brahman, which is called *svar* (heaven).

Because of the qualification "in the infinite" (*anante*), one might think that the word "infinite" could even be used figuratively for the triple heaven (*triviṣṭapa*); therefore, he says "in the eldest" (*jyeye*). In the eldest—that is, in the most excellent, the greatest of all, his own Self—he stands firmly established in the primary sense alone. The intention is that he does not, however, fall back into the cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). ||9||
Thus ends the fourth section. ||4||
